readings.roleRequirement: Explain why byte-verified text still needs record admission; explain how losing exclusion reasons and reporting only final totals hide actual rule populations; establish retained, rejected and withheld manual-review dispositions. State that the first reached rejecting or review rule supplies a terminal decision and stops evaluation, while surviving every rule yields retention with no first terminal rule; do not imply quality, privacy or permission approval.
readings.value: The problem: verified text is not yet training input A matching checksum tells us which text we have, not whether every record should enter a training corpus. A record may be malformed, too large for the processing budget, or contain a literal marker that our chosen policy excludes. Some records need review rather than an automatic yes or no. Deleting every excluded record without keeping its reason loses useful evidence. Reporting only the final retained count also hides which records each rule actually examined. If an early rule stops a record, later rules cannot truthfully report that the record passed or failed them. The solution here is an ordered filter with three dispositions: Retained: a candidate for the next data-processing stage, not a guarantee of quality, privacy or permission. Rejected: excluded by an automatic rule. Manual review: withheld from downstream training input. This example has no approval override. The first rule in the configured order that rejects a record or holds it for manual review supplies that record’s first terminal decision. Evaluation stops there; later rules are not evaluated for that record. If a record survives every rule, it is retained with no first terminal rule. The report preserves each record’s disposition, the rules actually evaluated, any first terminal rule and the record’s reference to its raw source. It does not copy excluded text into public findings.

readings.roleRequirement: Establish the eight course-authored records and two raw sources; specify whole-line marker framing, LF/CRLF/EOF boundaries, empty and failed-read behavior, literal payloads and byte counts; distinguish source provenance from final dataset splits and synthetic evidence from TinyStories filtering.
readings.value:
Eight records, with explicit boundaries Everything in the worked example is course-authored synthetic data. It is not a filtering result for TinyStories. The two source names fixture-train and fixture-validation preserve their raw-source provenance; they do not create the final training, validation or test split. The selected framing policy, end-of-input-delimited-v2, recognizes the ASCII marker <|endoftext|> only when it occupies an entire physical line. A marker line may end with LF, CRLF or end of input. Its bytes are a delimiter, not payload text. The same marker inside an ordinary text line is not a delimiter. End of input also closes a remaining nonempty payload, even without a final newline. End of input immediately after a separator creates no extra record. Consecutive separators create an empty payload that the filter can reject. A failed read is an error, not an end-of-input boundary. These rules are selected explicitly; the reader does not guess another format after a failure. For this fixture, append b"<|endoftext|>
" after every record below, in table order within each source. Every separator therefore contributes 14 bytes. In Rust literals, 
 denotes one LF byte and \xff one byte that is invalid as standalone UTF-8. Label | Source | Complete raw payload construction | Payload bytes | First terminal decision r0 | fixture-train | b"cat sat.
" | 9 | None; retained r1 | fixture-train | b"\xff
" | 2 | Strict UTF-8; rejected r2 | fixture-train | 65 copies of b'x', then b"
" | 66 | Raw size; rejected r3 | fixture-train | b"hi
" | 3 | Minimum normalized length; rejected r4 | fixture-validation | b"....
" | 5 | Minimum ASCII letters; rejected r5 | fixture-validation | b"demo-key=CANARY
" | 16 | Secret marker; rejected r6 | fixture-validation | b"contact=alex@example.invalid
" | 29 | Manual marker; held r7 | fixture-validation | b"demo-key=CANARY contact=alex@example.invalid
" | 45 | Secret marker; rejected The marker text and address are fictional inputs. Their presence in this table explains the lesson; it is not permission to include captured secrets or personal data in a real findings report.

readings.roleRequirement: Explain the fixture's seven ordered rules, thresholds and case policies; define CRLF replacement and edge trimming, UTF-8 byte lengths and the ASCII-share scalar denominator, exact comparison and zero-denominator review; distinguish the planned corpus policy and introduce the reached-population terminal fraction.
readings.value: The solution: stop once, count at every reached rule The fixture deliberately uses small thresholds so each failure is visible: Reject a raw payload above 64 bytes before decoding it. Reject invalid UTF-8. Normalize the decoded text and reject fewer than 4 normalized UTF-8 bytes. Reject fewer than 1 ASCII letter. Reject the literal demo-key=CANARY, matched without ASCII case distinctions. Hold the literal contact=, matched case-sensitively. Hold text below the configured ASCII-letter share. Normalization replaces CRLF pairs with LF, then trims only space, tab, CR and LF at the two edges. It preserves case, internal spaces and other Unicode characters. Length after normalization is measured in UTF-8 bytes, not characters or tokens. For the last rule, count Unicode scalar values other than the six ASCII whitespace characters: space, tab, LF, vertical tab, form feed and CR. The numerator counts ASCII letters among those values. Compare a configured fraction using checked integer cross-products, rather than rounding a floating-point ratio. A zero denominator is unavailable and sends a reached record to review; it is not an observed share of zero. The fixture’s threshold is 0/1, so its last survivor passes this rule. These thresholds are not the full-corpus policy. The planned corpus policy uses a 65{,}536-byte raw limit, at least 16 normalized bytes, at least 8 ASCII letters and an ASCII-letter share of at least 1/2, with its own selected marker lists. For example, the fixture’s short secret record would reach a different first terminal rule under a stricter length threshold. None of the fixture’s rates are measurements of a real corpus. For a named rule k, report its terminal fraction using the population that actually reached it: r_k=\frac{n_{\mathrm{disposition},k}}{n_{\mathrm{seen},k}}

readings.roleRequirement: Define every symbol in the terminal fraction, its dimensionless unit and unavailable zero-input state; explain two terminal decisions among four reached records versus among eight originals; relate shrinking stage populations and the retained/rejected/manual-review count conservation without merging review into rejection.
readings.value: Symbols in the filtering fraction k identifies a rule in the configured order. n_{\mathrm{seen},k} counts records surviving every earlier rule and reaching rule k. n_{\mathrm{disposition},k} counts reached records whose first terminal decision is rejection or a hold for review at rule k. r_k is dimensionless. When n_{\mathrm{seen},k}=0, the report stores unavailable, not zero. Four records reach the secret-marker rule, and it rejects two. Its terminal fraction is 2/4=1/2. Dividing by the original eight records gives 2/8=1/4, a different quantity: that rule’s terminal decisions as a fraction of all input records. Do not label the second quantity as the reached-population rate. The reached populations are 8,7,6,5,4,2,1, leaving one retained record. The final dispositions must conserve the input count: 8=1_{\mathrm{retained}}+6_{\mathrm{rejected}}+1_{\mathrm{manual\ review}} A binary exclusion summary gives 7 ineligible records, but those are 6 rejections plus 1 pending review. Calling all seven “rejected” discards the distinction needed to explain their outcomes.

readings.roleRequirement: Connect ordinary Read input and bounded framing to independently selected complete-source length/digest verification and provisional-output refusal; explain normalization and first-terminal filtering, the absent later result for r7, swapped dispositions and the limits of the two literal-marker heuristics.
readings.value:
Rust owns the framing and decisions The framer accepts an ordinary Read source. The output interface separates retained rows from body-free exclusion findings, without requiring a directory, filename, HTTP source or storage backend. Supporting libraries provide JSON encoding and SHA-256; the course code owns boundaries, rule order, terminal decisions and accounting. A bounded buffer retains only payloads within the selected size limit. An oversized record is drained to its boundary and counted without retaining its whole body. Read-buffer boundaries do not split records or invalidate a Unicode character: UTF-8 decoding happens on the complete bounded payload. Read the selected raw source completely and check its byte count and digest after framing. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch/src/data/stream.rs#source-bound-framing pub fn scan_source<R: Read, F>( reader: R, source: &SourceBinding, policy: &FramingPolicy, mut visit: F, ) -> Result<ScanSummary, DataError> where F: FnMut(Frame) -> Result<(), DataError>, { policy.validate()?; let limit = source.bytes().checked_add(1).ok_or(DataError::Overflow)?; let mut reader = reader.take(limit); let mut buffer = [0_u8; STREAM_BUFFER_BYTES]; let mut hasher = Sha256::new(); let mut observed = 0_u64; let mut framer = Framer::new(policy)?; loop { let length = reader.read(&mut buffer)?; if length == 0 { break; } observed = observed .checked_add(length as u64) .ok_or(DataError::Overflow)?; if observed > source.bytes() { return Err(DataError::SourceMismatch); } hasher.update(&buffer[..length]); for &byte in &buffer[..length] { framer.feed(byte, &mut visit)?; } } framer.finish(&mut visit)?; if observed != source.bytes() || format!("{:x}", hasher.finalize()) != source.file_sha256() { return Err(DataError::SourceMismatch); } Ok(framer.summary) } The raw source was selected independently before this read. A report succeeds only after the complete source’s observed length and digest agree with that selection. Rows emitted before that final check are provisional. A changed byte, truncated read or I/O error prevents publication of the completed result; a prefix must not become training input. Replace each CRLF pair with LF, then trim only space, tab, CR and LF from both text edges; preserve the remaining text. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch/src/data/filter.rs#narrow-normalization pub fn normalize(text: &str) -> String { text.replace("
", "
") .trim_matches([' ', '	', '', '
']) .to_owned() } For one record, evaluate the configured rules in order and stop at its first rejection or manual-review decision. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch/src/data/filter.rs#ordered-record-filter pub fn evaluate(frame: &Frame, policy: &FilterPolicy) -> Result<Decision, DataError> { policy.validate()?; let raw_bytes = frame.raw_bytes()?; let mut visited = vec![Rule::RawSize]; if raw_bytes > policy.framing.max_payload_bytes { return Ok(Decision::terminal(raw_bytes, visited, Rule::RawSize, None)); } let bytes = match &frame.data { FrameData::Bytes(bytes) if bytes.len() as u64 == raw_bytes => bytes, _ => return Err(DataError::InvalidRecord("frame body/span disagreement")), }; visited.push(Rule::Utf8); let text = match std::str::from_utf8(bytes) { Ok(text) => normalize(text), Err(_) => return Ok(Decision::terminal(raw_bytes, visited, Rule::Utf8, None)), }; let normalized_bytes = text.len() as u64; for &rule in &policy.stages[2..] { visited.push(rule); if normalized_terminal(&text, rule, policy)? { return Ok(Decision::terminal( raw_bytes, visited, rule, Some(normalized_bytes), )); } } Ok(Decision { disposition: Disposition::Retained, evaluated_rules: visited, first_terminal_rule: None, normalized_bytes: Some(normalized_bytes), raw_decoded: true, raw_bytes, retained_text: Some(text), }) } Record r7 contains both markers. With the secret rule first, it is rejected there; the manual-marker rule is not evaluated for that record. Swap those two rules and r7 is held for review instead. The new totals are one retained, five rejected and two pending review. The same raw bytes therefore produce different reasons and dispositions under different policies. Match secret-marker literals without ASCII case distinctions and manual-review literals case-sensitively; neither rule detects all sensitive text. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch/src/data/privacy.rs#literal-marker-decisions pub fn contains_ascii_case_insensitive(text: &str, markers: &[String]) -> bool { markers.iter().any(|marker| { !marker.is_empty() && text .as_bytes() .windows(marker.len()) .any(|window| window.eq_ignore_ascii_case(marker.as_bytes())) }) } pub fn contains_case_sensitive(text: &str, markers: &[String]) -> bool { markers .iter() .any(|marker| !marker.is_empty() && text.contains(marker)) } A quoted marker can cause a false positive. Sensitive text without a configured literal can pass. Likewise, few ASCII letters do not prove that a record is bad or that it is not English, and many ASCII letters do not establish language or quality. These heuristics need corpus-specific inspection, including inspection of excluded text under appropriate access controls.

readings.roleRequirement: Explain body-free findings, raw occurrence versus derived policy/artifact identity, bounded samples versus complete counters and metadata-budget refusal; distinguish physical, payload, delimiter, decoded and normalized byte totals; require independently selected retained eligibility and provide the synthetic demo command, setup and observable report.
readings.value: Preserve counts without exposing excluded bodies Increment a rule's seen count only when the record reaches it, then count survival or its first terminal decision. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch/src/data/governance.rs#stage-accounting fn record(&mut self, decision: &Decision, record_id: &str) -> Result<(), DataError> { for &rule in &decision.evaluated_rules { let stage = self .stages .iter_mut() .find(|stage| stage.rule == rule) .ok_or(DataError::InvalidRecord("unknown evaluated stage"))?; add(&mut stage.seen, 1)?; if decision.first_terminal_rule == Some(rule) { add(&mut stage.terminal, 1)?; } else { add(&mut stage.survived, 1)?; } } if decision.raw_decoded { add(&mut self.decoded_raw_bytes, decision.raw_bytes)?; } else { add(&mut self.undecoded_raw_bytes, decision.raw_bytes)?; } let normalized = decision.normalized_bytes.unwrap_or(0); add(&mut self.normalized_bytes, normalized)?; match decision.disposition { Disposition::Retained => { add(&mut self.retained, 1)?; add(&mut self.normalized_retained_bytes, normalized)?; } Disposition::Rejected => { add(&mut self.rejected, 1)?; add(&mut self.normalized_rejected_bytes, normalized)?; } Disposition::ManualReview => { add(&mut self.manual_review, 1)?; add(&mut self.normalized_manual_bytes, normalized)?; } } let sample = self .samples .iter_mut() .find(|group| { group.disposition == decision.disposition && group.first_terminal_rule == decision.first_terminal_rule }) .ok_or(DataError::InvalidRecord("sample group"))?; if sample.record_ids.len() < SAMPLE_REFERENCES_PER_GROUP { sample.record_ids.push(record_id.to_owned()); } Ok(()) } A finding contains a source reference, half-open raw byte span, occurrence ID, evaluated rule IDs and the terminal decision. It contains no excluded body, snippet or matched capture. The occurrence ID binds the selected raw artifact, source and payload IDs, raw file digest and span. Equal text at different spans has different occurrence IDs. A changed filter policy does not change those raw occurrence IDs, but does change the derived artifact’s policy identity. Per source and terminal reason, the report includes the first 32 occurrence IDs in input order as samples. The full finding stream and counters remain complete: the sample bound is not permission to stop counting. Findings and the receipt share a strict metadata budget below 100 MiB. Exceeding that budget fails the attempt; it does not silently truncate evidence. Byte accounting uses separate bases. Separator bytes are outside raw payload spans. Payloads rejected before decoding still contribute to the raw total. Normalized byte totals include only records actually decoded and normalized. A complete run reads 287 physical bytes: 175 payload bytes and 112 delimiter bytes. Of the payload bytes, 68 belong to records rejected before decoding and 107 are decoded. Normalization leaves 101 bytes across decoded records: 8 retained, 65 rejected and 28 pending review. These are byte counts, not token counts; excluded text still contributes to its applicable accounting totals. A retained row is checked again against the selected filtered artifact, policy, source references, span and text digest before consumption. Relabeling a manual-review payload or selecting an untrusted candidate’s own manifest does not make it eligible. Run the offline synthetic fixture and print the report derived from the Rust decisions. rust/demos/ch42-deterministic-corpus-filtering/src/main.rs#offline-filtering-example fn main() { match ch42_deterministic_corpus_filtering::demo_report().and_then(|report| { serde_json::to_string_pretty(&report).map_err(|_| { llm_from_scratch::functional::data::stream::DataError::InvalidRecord( "report serialization", ) }) }) { Ok(report) => println!("{report}"), Err(error) => { eprintln!("filter fixture failed: {error}"); std::process::exit(1); } } } To reproduce the example, start at the repository root with Docker installed and the course development image available. This command uses only synthetic bytes, so the corpus download is disabled: COURSE_CORPUS=false ./course run cargo run --offline --locked -p ch42-deterministic-corpus-filtering The JSON report records eight inputs, one retained record, six rejected records and one pending-review record, plus each rule’s reached count and terminal fraction. Its changed-order comparison records one retained, five rejected and two pending review. Artifact digests identify the actual policy and source bytes; do not replace them with illustrative hashes.

readings.roleRequirement: State the bounded C4 exclusion and RefinedWeb filtering/deduplication claims with their primary citations; distinguish aggregate corpus/model evidence from this fixture and identify the binary exclusion code as a course-local loss-of-information contrast, not a reproduction of either paper or a quality/privacy guarantee.
readings.value: History: inspect what filtering removes A binary keep/drop report hides the reason for exclusion and the population that each later rule actually inspected. The C4 study examines text removed by filters; RefinedWeb later combines filtering and deduplication in a web-scale corpus. Dodge and colleagues inspect C4 exclusions and find disproportionate removal of content concerning minority groups by its word blocklist. Their 2021 Documenting Large Webtext Corpora: A Case Study on the Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus motivates examining removals rather than assuming that a filter is neutral. Penedo and colleagues describe a large web corpus built with filtering and deduplication, and evaluate language models trained on its data. Their 2023 RefinedWeb paper concerns a much broader pipeline than this eight-record fixture. Its model results do not certify our heuristics or isolate a benefit from one rule. The Rust contrast below is course-local: it reduces our existing decisions to one exclusion bit. It is not an implementation reproduced from either paper. It counts seven excluded records but loses their rejection-versus-review distinction and cannot say which later rule saw each one. Reduce the fixture's three dispositions to one exclusion bit and expose the information that summary omits. rust/demos/ch42-deterministic-corpus-filtering/src/lib.rs#binary-filter-contrast /// A course-local reporting contrast, not either paper's implementation. pub fn binary_exclusion(disposition: Disposition) -> bool { disposition != Disposition::Retained } Record explicit exclusions and stage populations before deduplication and training; a passed heuristic is not a quality, privacy or memorization guarantee.

readings.value: Optional practice: inspect the recorded evidence Source withdrawal is a known-lineage calculation Filtering also preserves source lineage so a later withdrawal can identify recorded downstream artifacts. The separate fictional graph uses r0 as a raw-source node alias, not as the worked table’s record label or an actual occurrence digest. Its descendants are a0, f0, s0, tok0 and w0. Two paths reach w0; the result lists it once. The unrelated branch f9 belongs to a different source and is not in this withdrawal’s descendant set. Validate the supplied lineage graph, then list each known descendant of the selected raw source once; this does not erase stored data. rust/crates/llm-from-scratch/src/data/deletion.rs#known-descendant-withdrawal pub fn withdrawal( &self, raw_roots: &[String], limits: GraphLimits, ) -> Result<WithdrawalPlan, DataError> { let kinds = self.validate(limits)?; let mut reached = BTreeSet::new(); let mut pending = BTreeSet::new(); for root in raw_roots { if kinds.get(root.as_str()) != Some(&NodeKind::RawSource) { return Err(DataError::InvalidGraph("unknown or non-source root")); } pending.insert(root.as_str()); } while let Some(id) = pending.pop_first() { if !reached.insert(id) { continue; } for edge in &self.edges { if edge.parent == id && !reached.contains(edge.child.as_str()) { pending.insert(edge.child.as_str()); } } } let mut artifacts = Vec::new(); let mut sources = Vec::new(); for id in reached { match kinds.get(id) { Some(NodeKind::RawSource) => sources.push(id.into()), Some(NodeKind::Artifact) => artifacts.push(id.into()), None => return Err(DataError::InvalidGraph("unknown reached node")), } } Ok(WithdrawalPlan { artifacts, sources }) } Run these commands from the repository root with Docker installed and running. With the secret-marker rule first, r7 is rejected and never reaches the manual-marker rule. With the manual-marker rule first, r7 is held for review and never reaches the secret-marker rule. The raw source and occurrence identities do not change. The derived policy and artifact identities change because the ordered filtering policy is different. The descendant set contains a0, f0, s0, tok0 and w0, with w0 listed once despite its two incoming paths; it excludes the unrelated f9. This calculation neither deletes stored bytes nor unlearns a trained model. It cannot discover unrecorded copies. The graph’s checkpoint-like node is fictional; this example has not trained a model.
